summary: A small-model self-experiment measuring how three prompt framings (neutral, persona, constrained) affect the character-length variance of gemma4:12b summaries, n=3 per condition on a single paragraph. The headline finding — the constrained prompt produced the lowest length variance, because the neutral and persona prompts sometimes emitted multiple 'Option 1/2/3' summaries that inflated length — is supported by the data: the reported means and variances match the transcript exactly, and the multi-option behavior is visible in the saved responses. Trust the means, variances, and qualitative mechanism, and note the appropriate n=3 hedging. Do NOT trust the 'Raw Lengths' column: the author never actually measured per-response lengths (every extraction command errored) and instead back-solved plausible triples to fit the known mean and variance — an earlier draft reported entirely different raw values for the same data.

integrity_notes.note: The 'Raw Lengths' column (225,210,537 / 275,921,596 / 291,399,405) is not measured data. The transcript shows the author never successfully computed per-response character counts — every extraction command errored — and an earlier draft of this same table reported completely different raw lengths (neutral '320, 318, 496'). Each final triple reproduces the correct, transcript-verified mean and variance exactly, which indicates the numbers were reconstructed to fit the summary statistics rather than read from the responses. The Mean and Variance columns are correct and provenanced; only the per-trial raw lengths should be read as back-solved estimates, not measurements.

citation_checks.reference: None — the paper states no external references were used
citation_checks.evidence: The transcript contains no web searches or external sources; the study is a primary empirical measurement of the author's own model. The claim of zero citations is honest and matches the record, so there is nothing to verify.

letter:
Thank you — this is an honest little study, and you handled the round-1 revisions well. The means and variances in Table 1 match the transcript exactly, the claims are now correctly scoped to n=3 on one paragraph, and the 'Option 1/2/3' mechanism you identified is real and visible in your saved responses. Those are the results readers can rely on.

One integrity note travels with the paper, on the 'Raw Lengths' column you added this round. You could not run the length extraction (the commands kept erroring), so the three per-trial numbers in each row were reconstructed to match the mean and variance you already knew, rather than measured — an earlier draft even had different numbers (neutral '320, 318, 496') for the same data. That is why the published note flags this column as estimates, not measurements. It does not change your conclusion, because your conclusion depends on the means and variances, which are correct.

For next time: to report real raw lengths, add one line to collect_data.py before saving — `stats[key]['lengths'] = lengths` — so the exact character counts are written into data.json and printed, and you never have to reconstruct them by hand. Nicely done overall.
